title: The 403 from serverless
outcome: Classic clusters could read the firewalled storage account and serverless couldn't; the old way of allowing serverless had stopped working.

content.bookmark: Serverless compute runs in Databricks' account, not your VNet. To reach a firewalled storage account, allow the AzureDatabricksServerless service tag through a network security perimeter, or add a private endpoint in an NCC.

check.prompt: Where does serverless compute run in Azure Databricks?
options: In the workspace's injected VNet, next to the classic clusters in your subscription
In a serverless compute plane in the Azure Databricks account, in the workspace's region
In the control plane's web application
check.why: Classic compute runs in your subscription's VNet; serverless runs in a serverless compute plane in the Azure Databricks account, in the workspace's region.

check.prompt: What is a network connectivity configuration (NCC)?
options: An account-level, regional construct that manages private endpoints for serverless compute
A per-cluster setting for classic compute
check.why: An NCC is created by account admins, is regional, can be attached to up to 50 workspaces in the region, and manages serverless private endpoints.

check.prompt: A private endpoint is added in an NCC for a storage account. What has to happen before it works?
options: Nothing: it is active at once
Databricks support approves it after a review of the storage account
The storage account's owner accepts the request
check.why: Adding a private endpoint creates a request the resource owner must accept.

check.prompt: Does allowing serverless through a storage firewall also allow classic compute?
options: No: classic compute must be allowed separately
Yes, both use the same rule
Only when secure cluster connectivity is enabled on the workspace
check.why: A storage firewall affects classic compute too, and classic compute must be allowed separately.

caseStudy.setting: An energy company (fictional) has a VNet-injected Azure Databricks workspace. Its ADLS Gen2 account has a firewall that allows the workspace's subnets, and a rule added last year that allow-listed serverless subnet IDs. Unity Catalog reaches the account through an Access Connector's managed identity.

events.what: Analysts move their dashboards to a serverless SQL warehouse. Queries on tables in the firewalled account fail with 403 Forbidden.
The same queries work from a classic cluster. The storage team says nothing changed on their side.
The platform team finds that storage accounts that allow-listed serverless subnet IDs can no longer connect, and has to choose a supported approach.

pipeline: Serverless SQL warehouse · runs in the serverless compute plane
Classic clusters · in the workspace's injected VNet
ADLS Gen2 · firewall allows workspace subnets and old serverless subnet IDs
Unity Catalog · storage credential from an Access Connector
tasks: Why did classic work and serverless fail?
Which approach would you choose to allow serverless?

debrief.title: Why classic worked and serverless didn't
text: Classic compute runs in the workspace's own VNet, whose subnets the firewall allows. Serverless runs in Databricks' account, outside that VNet, so the subnet rule doesn't cover it.
The rule meant for serverless allow-listed serverless subnet IDs, and the docs say such storage accounts can no longer connect. Without a supported rule, serverless gets 403 Forbidden.

debrief.title: Supported options
text: Network security perimeter: put the storage account in a perimeter and allow the AzureDatabricksServerless service tag, which can be scoped to a region.

Private endpoint: an account admin creates an NCC in the region, adds a private endpoint rule for the storage account, the storage owner accepts it, and the NCC is attached to the workspace. It needs the Premium plan.
Either way, keep the classic subnets allowed separately: a storage firewall applies to both kinds of compute.

debrief.title: Choosing
text: A private endpoint keeps the traffic private but adds limits to plan for (NCCs per region, endpoints per region) and a networking charge for serverless traffic to customer resources. The service tag is simpler to run.
Make the choice part of the platform's network design, so the next serverless workload doesn't rediscover the problem.

takeaway: Serverless isn't in your VNet: firewall rules for your subnets don't cover it.
Allowing serverless subnet IDs no longer works; use a network security perimeter or an NCC private endpoint.
Allow classic and serverless compute separately.
content.honesty: If you haven't configured Azure Databricks networking, say so, and explain where classic and serverless compute run and how serverless reaches firewalled storage. If you have, describe the design you chose.

tasks: What should have been checked before moving dashboards to serverless?
How would you plan the next move to serverless?

debrief.title: Before moving
text: Whether serverless can reach every storage account the dashboards read.

debrief.title: Next move
text: A connectivity check per data source as part of the migration plan.

sayIt.question: How do you plan a platform change that users will notice if it goes wrong?
points: List what the change depends on, including network and security.
Test with real data sources before switching users.
Have a way back.
Tell users what changes and when.
Check results after the switch.

tasks: What do you tell the analysts?
What decision do you need from whom?

debrief.title: Analysts
text: Use the classic warehouse or cluster for now; serverless will work once the storage access rule is replaced, by a stated date.

debrief.title: Decision
text: Security and networking choose between a network security perimeter and a private endpoint; the platform team implements.

sayIt.question: A migration is blocked by a security rule. How do you move it forward?
points: Find the exact rule and why it blocks.
Bring the right owners together quickly.
Present supported options with their trade-offs.
Keep users working on the old path meanwhile.
Record the decision for future migrations.

tasks: How do you sequence the change?

debrief.title: People
text: An account admin (NCC), the storage owner (accepting the endpoint or the perimeter rule), and security.

debrief.title: Sequence
text: Agree the approach, configure it in a test workspace, apply to production, then remove the old subnet-ID rule.

sayIt.question: How do you coordinate a change that needs several teams' approvals?
points: Name every team and the approval each gives.
Agree the plan once, together.
Test the change before production.
Track approvals to avoid waiting.
Remove obsolete configuration afterwards.

tasks: How would you set up the private endpoint option?

debrief.title: Private endpoint
text: In the account console, create an NCC in the workspace's region, add a private endpoint rule for the storage account, have the storage owner approve it, and attach the NCC to the workspace.

debrief.title: Verifying
text: A query from the serverless warehouse reads the table; the classic cluster still works; the old subnet-ID rule is removed.

sayIt.question: Explain how Azure Databricks compute reaches a firewalled storage account.
points: Classic compute runs in your VNet; allow its subnets (service or private endpoints).
Serverless runs in Databricks' account, in the workspace's region.
For serverless: a network security perimeter allowing AzureDatabricksServerless, or a private endpoint in an NCC.
The storage owner accepts NCC private endpoints.
Allow-listing serverless subnet IDs no longer works.
